## Breaking down our economic impact

To understand the scale of what we can achieve together, today we're releasing Google’s 2025 EU Economic Impact Report , commissioned by Google and developed by Implement Consulting Group. The report shows how Google’s products and platforms, investments in infrastructure, and Cloud and AI technologies contributed more than €200 billion to EU GDP. - Products and platforms (approx €157 billion): Tools like Search, Ads, Android, Google Play, Chrome, and YouTube connect millions of European businesses to global markets, allow creators to monetize content, and help citizens access essential information and services.

- AI and Cloud (approx €32 billion): Cloud services and artificial intelligence help European enterprises, public institutions, and developers scale infrastructure, optimize operations, and build new capabilities securely within Europe.

- Infrastructure and offices (approx €11B): Our data centers, offices and operations generate direct economic value through local procurement, supply-chain partnerships, and community investments.

## Productivity gains

AI productivity gains aren't hypothetical; they're happening across the continent right now. Recent findings by the European Investment Bank show AI is helping to lift labor productivity by an average of 4% across adopting firms without displacing employment.

Take Renault Group. Amidst the rising costs and production pressures of today’s automotive sector, Renault Group is using Google AI to modernize its manufacturing operations and secure their competitiveness. On the factory floor, AI is preventing breakdowns and detecting manufacturing defects in real time, cutting factory downtime and production defects in half. Before this deployment, floor technicians focused the majority of their time hunting for errors rather than fixing them. AI completely flipped the script, turning firefighters into engineers. This shift in efficiency at Renault Group is driving between 100 and 120 million euros in annual savings.

Looking ahead, AI could boost the European economy by €1.2 trillion annually within a decade. But to deliver on this promise, Europe needs a predictable, supportive regulatory environment that champions business success and unlocks growth rather than stifling innovation. It also requires equipping people with the tools to succeed, like Danilly. Since 2014, Google has trained over 13 million people in the EU on essential digital and AI skills.

Google's journey in Europe started 25 years ago with our first employee in Hamburg and has grown to a footprint of 26 offices across 17 member states and eight data centers, supporting over 100,000 European jobs. Our relationship with Europe is one of partnership — we live here, we build here, we’re part of the communities we serve across the continent.

We remain dedicated to working with European institutions, businesses, and communities to ensure this wave of innovation drives inclusive and sustainable growth across the continent.

# Ask a Scientist: How are researchers using AI to help pregnant women access ultrasounds?

In a recent study, healthcare workers were trained to perform simpler ultrasounds and used AI to interpret the results, enabling Google researchers to help more people get the prenatal ultrasounds they need. We sat down with an OB/GYN physician and AI researcher on the team to learn more.

Lindsey Lanquist

Contributor

Google researchers are using artificial intelligence to bridge the global gap in prenatal care. By training healthcare workers to perform simple "blind sweep" ultrasounds, the team’s machine learning model can accurately determine gestational age and fetal position without needing a specialized sonographer. This portable, offline-capable technology offers a promising way to provide life-saving diagnostic information to women in under-resourced areas.

Ultrasounds give women crucial information during pregnancy — they allow expecting parents to hear a heartbeat, count fingers and toes, check how many babies there are, see how they’re positioned, and so much more. But not every pregnancy gets this level of care. About two-thirds of people across the globe lack ready access to diagnostic imaging services, like ultrasounds and X-rays. And there aren’t enough sonographers to perform ultrasounds for everyone who needs them. So what do you do if you can’t get an ultrasound where you live?

Google researchers explored an AI tool for this problem through a research study with Northwestern and Jacarand Health. The research involved training healthcare workers to perform simple “blind sweep” ultrasounds and used machine learning models to interpret the results. With this approach, they were able to detect important prenatal information, like gestational age and fetal presentation, as accurately as a trained sonographer, giving women in under-resourced areas better information about what to expect ahead of one of the most significant events of their lives.

We sat down with Googlers Angelica Willis and Dr. Nichole Young-Lin to learn more about this research — and what it could mean for the potential future of ultrasound access worldwide.

What do you do at Google?

Angelica: I’m a software engineer and AI researcher. I’ve always been passionate about using AI for social good and healthcare equity. When we look at maternal care, technical advancements are only as valuable as the lives they impact. My motivation is building technology that actually reaches the people who need it most. And right now, my focus is making healthcare more accessible worldwide.

Nichole: I’m the in-house obstetrician-gynecologist (OB/GYN) at Google. I actually got my start in public health researching postpartum hemorrhage to reduce maternal mortality. That inspired me to become a doctor, but I soon realized that to address global inequities in medical access, we need the scale that technology can offer. I now work on a range of women’s health and consumer health projects at Google while continuing to care for patients.

Why are ultrasounds so important?

Nichole: As an OB/GYN, we turn to ultrasounds for all sorts of questions. Is the baby growing appropriately? Are there anomalies? And we rely on early ultrasounds, in particular, to estimate gestational age: How far along is the pregnancy, and when is the baby due? Screenings, treatment, management, and being able to prepare for a safe delivery — that all depends on a timeline determined by gestational age.

Many people have irregular periods or don’t track their periods, so we can’t always rely on period history to estimate gestational age. And there can be serious ramifications for getting it wrong. Let’s say someone needs to deliver early because of a complication. You think you’re delivering a 37-week baby, but maybe you’re actually delivering a 34-week baby with less mature lungs. Those babies need very different levels of care when they’re born. When we’re able to accurately define the baby’s gestational age, we’re much better prepared to provide both the baby and the mother with the support they need after birth.

What’s keeping people from getting ultrasounds during pregnancy?

Nichole: Traditional ultrasound machines are bulky and expensive, creating a barrier to access. When they break in remote clinics, there’s often no one to fix them, and they require stable electricity when they do work. With recent developments in handheld ultrasound devices, we’ve seen greater potential for us to get ultrasounds to more women, especially in low-resource settings. The handheld machines are smaller and cheaper, and many are battery-powered, so they’re portable and easily accessible

Angelica: But even with advancements in portable device technology, it still takes two years of intense hands-on training to become a sonographer, resulting in a global shortage of sonographers who can perform prenatal ultrasounds.

Tell me about your research. What are you doing differently to solve those problems?

Angelica: We partnered with Jacaranda Health and Northwestern Medicine in our study of 1,000 mothers in Nairobi, Kenya, and 1,000 more in Chicago. We found our machine learning model could detect gestational age and fetal presentation as accurately as a trained sonographer.

In a traditional ultrasound, the sonographer has to move the probe around precisely to get specific measurements. And it’s really hard to get right. Our research involved a “blind sweep” ultrasound instead. Operators sweep the probe over the abdomen in a predefined pattern. And healthcare workers who’ve never performed an ultrasound before can learn how to do it in eight hours.

These blind sweep operators gather videos that help us get the imaging we need of the baby, and we built an AI model to analyze those videos. It can tell the operator if they need to redo the sweep. And it can estimate gestational age and indicate fetal presentation — what position the baby’s in. Crucially, all of that processing happens on the device, so it doesn’t require an electricity supply or even Wi-Fi to be able to provide the operator and the mother with the insights they need to prepare for birth.

What could this mean for maternal healthcare worldwide?

Angelica: We saw this project as an opportunity to demonstrate what’s possible in maternal healthcare. The research proves we can broaden access to expert-level care and put it directly into the hands of frontline community health workers.

Nichole: The goal of our research is to show how expanded access to life-saving ultrasound care could impact communities, and we’re getting there one step at a time. Through this research, we’ve made huge strides toward showing that this is a viable application of AI in maternal healthcare because we can use it across different patient populations and healthcare settings. But why stop at gestational age and fetal presentation — or even maternal healthcare? Ultrasound can be used for so many things, like seeing how much someone is bleeding after an accident or an injury. There’s so much potential for AI to help improve maternal health and healthcare across the board.

## The "magic state" bottleneck

Since 2004, long before quantum computing was a practical engineering pursuit, researchers have foreseen a particularly tricky bottleneck.

To achieve “universal” quantum computing and execute useful programs, you need to be able to run (and error-correct ) a specific set of quantum operations. You can do this by first creating what are called "magic states," so dubbed because they can help you create the operations you need for going beyond classical computing.

But there’s a catch: creating high-quality, error-corrected magic states is incredibly resource-heavy. Some estimates have shown that up to 95% of a quantum computer’s entire capacity might need to be dedicated to making them — leaving little room for actual computing. An extra challenge is that once you use a magic state, you can’t re-use it, making magic states a scarce resource.

So for 20 years, researchers have been chipping away at this cost of magic, bringing it lower and lower.

## How we made this breakthrough

In 2024, Google Quantum AI researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones harnessed an idea from the literature, refined it, and developed what we now call “magic state cultivation.” Their approach promised an especially large reduction. The idea was that cultivation would act like a filter. You would inject a noisy state into a small region on a quantum chip, and then run a series of highly coordinated measurements to check for errors and remove any flawed attempts. Craig and team showed how that would let you grow, or “cultivate,” an exceptionally pure, low-error quantum state that you could simultaneously adapt into a larger, useful encoding.

On paper, it looked great. If we could make this idea actually work on our quantum hardware, it could substantially reduce the size of the quantum computer needed for practical tasks.

In practice — and on par with developing many new technologies — it required a whole series of technical innovations and engineering.

As just one example, when first testing the cultivation protocol, Google Quantum AI research scientist Emma Rosenfeld was seeing data that seemed to defy the laws of physics. After months of confusion, simulations, discussions with colleagues, and consistency checks, she found that it arose from an incorrect assumption in the team’s go-to measurement technique. Specifically, a particular kind of noise in the lab caused by electrical equipment drift and temperature variation was interfering with the benchmark’s validity. The solution required a pivot in both our theoretical and engineering approaches. The team added extra control to the system to reduce the impact of that noise, and invented a new benchmarking technique to solve the issue more fundamentally, by using cultivation as a tool to measure itself.

With this and many more algorithmic innovations and engineering solutions, we established a new state-of-the-art in quantum metrology. On Google Quantum AI's Willow processor, our protocol achieved an extraordinary 40-fold reduction in errors relative to un-cultivated states. And we got T-states with a record logical fidelity of 99.99%.

Now published in Science , this work is the first demonstration of a practical solution to one of quantum computing's most severe resource bottlenecks. It demonstrates, on real hardware, that we can efficiently create these crucial magic states.

## Our findings and the future

We also took the first steps in demonstrating that Craig and others’ theories are compatible with our quantum computing architecture. We learned how to successfully switch between “color codes” (one newer type of quantum error correction, ideal for cultivation) and “surface codes” (another, more established method), grafting states from a distance-3 color code to a distance-5 surface code. Originally developed in the 2024 theory paper, this grafting protocol showed that in practice, purified states can survive and transfer smoothly inside our hardware.

Of course, we still need to demonstrate magic state cultivation at a larger scale to make it realistic for practical quantum computing, and plenty of technical challenges remain. But this achievement takes a key theoretical idea and turns it into an experimentally demonstrated reality. It brings us one step closer to our goal at Google Quantum AI : building a useful, error-corrected quantum computer to solve otherwise unsolvable problems.

PDFM combines aggregated search trends and mobility and environmental patterns into a dynamic, high-resolution picture of a community. Partners can integrate these insights directly into their own systems.

- Boosting timely disease prediction (cardiovascular disease): By integrating real-time population signals into chronic disease models, researchers at NYU Langone Health projected same-year cardiovascular mortality with similar — and in some cases improved — performance over conventional approaches. The faster these insights are generated, the faster they can be used to direct critical resources to vulnerable communities.

- Tracking cross-border immunization (measles, mumps and rubella): Researchers at Mount Sinai Health System and Boston Children’s Hospital incorporated human behavioral patterns on either side of the U.S.-Canada border to gain a more accurate view of vaccination rates in U.S. counties and uncover insights that could be overlooked by traditional public health models.

- Anticipating seasonal surges (dengue): Many endemic diseases exhibit seasonal fluctuations tied to environmental and weather shifts. Combining PDFM with localized climate models allowed researchers at the University of Oxford and Tecnológico de Monterrey to more accurately forecast dengue fever outbreaks across Mexico. This can provide vital lead time to take early action, such as killing mosquito larvae.

This could help frontline teams take proactive measures.
